verdict: CONFIRMED-BUT-SCOPED: the supplied fixed datasets, trace and independent reference results are internally consistent and, taken at face value, establish a reproducible canonicalization-invariance failure for this exact input pair in upstream rdf-canon 0.15.3, whose proximate cause is an unresolved tie between two structurally distinguishable blank nodes at RDFC-1.0 §4.4.3(5.3). The evidence supports classifying this as shared-algorithm underdetermination rather than a proven Rust-only coding error, but it does NOT establish an accepted standards erratum, does not close the root-cause search, and does not justify any production change. No patch exists; none is approved. Repository should remain blocked pending owner decision; the smallest responsible next step is read-only evidence completion plus upstream/W3C reproducer filing.
evidence_assessment: I re-derived the load-bearing claims by hand from the packet rather than accepting them. (1) ISOMORPHISM: dataset(labels) is applied with b0->zz0, b2->zz4, b3->zz3, b4->zz5 (b1,b5 unused); this is injective on the four occurring labels, quad positions and IRIs are preserved, and the three quads are distinct, so 'original' and 'renamed' are the same RDF dataset up to blank node renaming. Byte-different canonical outputs are therefore a genuine violation of label-independence, not a comparison artifact. (2) TOPOLOGY: the only candidate permutation exchanging b2,b3 that maps Q1 to Q3 is sigma = (b2 b3)(b0 b4); it maps the sole p-quad 'b4 p b0' to 'b0 p b4', which is not present. sigma = (b2 b3) with b0,b4 fixed maps Q1 to 'b4 q b3 g b2', also absent. Hence no automorphism exchanges b2 and b3; topology-proof.json is correct and the tie is not justified by genuine symmetry. (3) H1 EQUALITY is expected, not anomalous: under the a/z abstraction of §4.6.3 both nodes' mention sets serialize to the same sorted multiset {'_:z <q> _:a _:z .','_:z <q> _:z _:a .'}. (4) Hn EQUALITY: for top-level b2 the related components are b4(s,<q>,canonical c14n1), b0(s,<q>,c14n0), b3 twice (g with H1, o with <q>+H1); for top-level b3 they are b4(s), b0(s), b2 twice (o with <q>+H1, g with H1). Because §4.7.3 hashes each component independently and §4.8.3(3.1.2) files it into Hn keyed only by that hash, the intra-quad correlation 'which anchor co-occurs with which position' is discarded, and the two key sets coincide exactly (0feea/a62dd/dad1b/fcc96). The recursive calls are likewise mirror images and yield e0920..., producing byte-identical top-level preimages and hash a812f907... for all four calls. The trace's four Hn lines and four nd lines are consistent with this derivation. (5) TRACE FAITHFULNESS: the diff adds only eprintln!; the log's first four h1/issue lines correspond exactly to the two single-edge positive-control runs (distinct H1 values 0dffb95/70eaaa6 vs 84e1a25/ae1d96e in the full run), the h1 emission order is code-point-sorted over original labels (b0,b2,b3,b4 and zz0,zz3,zz4,zz5), and the chosen-path strings match §4.8.3(5.4.4.2.2)/(5.4.5.2)/(5.4.5.3) exactly. This internal coherence is strong evidence the instrumentation is non-perturbing, though I cannot verify it independently. (6) OUTPUT CHECK: I verified each Rust output is a valid relabeling of its input quad-by-quad; the sole difference is which of the tied pair receives c14n2 vs c14n3. (7) MECHANISM: hash_path_list holds two entries with equal hash and different issuer maps; Vec::sort is stable, so the winner is the first-inserted, i.e. the identifier_list order, which the trace shows is derived from a label-ordered map. The decisive under-specification is therefore §4.4.3 step 3 ('For each key n in the blank node to quads map' - iteration order undefined) combined with the tie in step 5.3 ('code point ordered by the hash' - tie order undefined). The report maps §4.7.3, §4.8.3(3.1.x) and §4.4.3(5.2-5.3) correctly but under-weights step 3, which is where the label leak actually enters. (8) REFERENCE: the JS results reproduce exactly the same two candidate outputs (d426d... equals the Rust 'original' string; 7807... equals the Rust 'renamed' string), so both implementations are choosing between the identical two tie resolutions. JS same-order relabel agreement is not evidence of label-independence: JS inherits first-appearance order from quad order, and the supplied relabeling preserves first-appearance order, so agreement is expected; the 5.0.0 12-case matrix (2 distinct outputs split strictly by quad order) confirms JS is order-dependent instead. (9) DIAGNOSTIC LIMITS: the JS divergence is visible only at maxDeepIterations 16 / timeout 1000; both defaults reject the pair at 2 deep iterations, and the packet correctly disclaims any default-safe claim. Budgets are non-normative mitigations (§7.1), so raising them is a legitimate way to observe the normative algorithm - but it means the deployed JS default fails closed on this input while the Rust default evidently returned output. That asymmetry, not a JS output bug, is the practically distinguishing fact.

The harness links only oxrdf and rdf_canon::canonicalize_quads; PR 6095, the failing Sparq property test, the CI counterexample fixture, the dependency path (direct/vendored/fork) and downstream consumers of the canonical bytes are entirely absent from the packet.

blocking_findings.finding: Classification is shared-algorithm underdetermination, not a demonstrated Rust-only defect. Both quoted implementations follow their normative steps; the divergence enters through two orderings the Recommendation leaves undefined (§4.4.3 step 3 map iteration; §4.4.3 step 5.3 tie order). Any local tie-break rule that picks one of the two candidates would change canonical output relative to other conforming implementations for inputs where they currently agree with us.
blocking_findings.evidence: canon.rs 342-391 (stable sort, insertion order = label order); RDFC10Sync.js 129-164 (insertion order = quad order); normative text quoted for 4.4.3 (3), (5.3), 4.7.3, 4.8.3.
blocking_findings.required_action: File a minimal reproducer upstream (zkp-ld/rdf-canon) and with w3c/rdf-canon after a prior-art search, and obtain maintainer/WG response before considering any output-selecting change. Unilateral tie-break selection is out of scope.

blocking_findings.finding: Blanket rejection of tied N-degree results would break conforming behavior on genuine symmetry. In test021c (circle of 2) the two results also carry equal hashes and different issuer maps, yet both tie resolutions serialize identically.
blocking_findings.evidence: reference-fixtures.json #test021c; §4.4.3 non-normative note ('this only occurs when there are isomorphisms ... would appear the same').
blocking_findings.required_action: Any fail-closed rule must be conditioned on divergence of the resulting serialization, not on the existence of a tie, and must be proven no-op on the full W3C suite before it is even proposed.

blocking_findings.finding: Conformance coverage is far too thin to bound blast radius. Three of the suite's fixtures were run, only on the JS reference; the Rust upstream test suite was not executed at all, and no randomized differential campaign exists.

blocking_findings.required_action: Produce an unmodified-baseline run of the complete W3C RDFC-1.0 suite against rdf-canon 0.15.3 and against the JS reference, plus a bounded randomized order/relabel differential campaign, before any repair option is scored.

blocking_findings.finding: The Rust budget behaviour is unquantified. The JS reference rejects this 3-quad, 4-blank-node input under defaults, while Rust apparently accepted it under its default HndqCallCounter. Whether an ambiguity-triggered error would be a new rejection class in Rust is therefore unknown.
blocking_findings.evidence: reference-replay.json default errors ('Maximum deep iterations exceeded (2)') vs replay.log producing full canonical output; canon.rs 707-708 call_counter.add.
blocking_findings.required_action: Document Rust's default call-limit semantics and the set of currently-accepted inputs, so that any fail-closed proposal can state exactly which inputs change from success to typed error.

blocking_findings.finding: An unverified secondary Rust deviation was not considered by the diagnosis: §4.4.3(5.3.1) requires issuing canonical identifiers 'in the same order' as the temporary identifiers were issued, but the code rebuilds a BTreeMap keyed by the temporary identifier string, which orders 'b10' before 'b2'. The JS reference uses getOldIds() insertion order. This cannot explain the present counterexample (temporary ids never exceed b1) but, if real, is an independent Rust-specific conformance divergence.
blocking_findings.required_action: Inspect IdentifierIssuer::issued_identifiers_map, and construct a fixture in which one hash-path result issues at least eleven temporary identifiers; compare Rust and reference. Report separately; do not conflate with this issue.

blocking_findings.finding: Asymmetric test matrix. Rust was tested only for relabeling at one quad order; the reference was tested for both. The claim that Rust is order-invariant (implied by BTreeMap keying) is untested, and Rust's input type is a quad slice whose duplicate/order semantics are not evidenced.
blocking_findings.evidence: harness/src/main.rs runs one order per labeling; 5.0.0 supplement covers 12 JS cases only.
blocking_findings.required_action: Run the full 12-case order x labeling matrix on unmodified rdf-canon 0.15.3 and record whether Rust is order-invariant, label-invariant, or neither.

nonblocking_findings: N1: canon.rs 978 and 1057 use 'path >= chosen_path' where the normative text says 'greater than'. Because path strings only grow by appending and a proper extension is code-point-greater than its prefix, the early skip on equality appears behaviourally inert, and the report is right that it cannot explain this input; still, it is a textual deviation that deserves its own note and test.

N2: The JS 'same-order relabel equal' result should not be reported as label-invariance. It follows from the relabeling preserving first-appearance order; a relabeling that also flips first-appearance order is expected to break it. Constructing that case would sharpen the shared-defect claim.

N3: The invariant actually contradicted is stated in a non-normative note in §4.4.3 and in §2's conformance framing ('consistently reproduce the same canonical identifiers'), not in a numbered MUST step. This materially weakens any 'the specification is violated' phrasing.

N4: The errata snapshot is label-filtered and explicitly non-exhaustive. Issue #217 ('isomorphic' vs 'same ignoring blank node identifiers') is adjacent terminology only and must not be cited as covering this.
N5: Provenance gaps: no oxrdf version/lockfile, no Rust archive hash, no toolchain record in the packet (held locally). Attach them to the reproducer so a third party can rebuild byte-identically.

N6: Consulting the partition-refinement/canonical-labelling literature (e.g. Hogan on canonical forms for isomorphic RDF graphs) before any algorithmic proposal is advisable; hash-refinement plus permutation search is known to require care where refinement stalls.
standard_level_claim: PROVISIONAL, NOT ACCEPTED. Three-way classification: (a) Rust-specific defect - not established for this counterexample; rdf-canon 0.15.3 appears to follow the quoted normative steps, and its label-dependence enters through orderings the Recommendation leaves undefined. One candidate Rust-specific deviation (B6, temporary-id ordering at 5.3.1) is unverified and cannot explain this input. (b) Shared algorithm behaviour - supported: two structurally non-equivalent blank nodes (no automorphism exchanges them) receive byte-identical N-degree preimages and hashes, so §4.4.3(5.3) is left to break a tie it cannot break by hash, and both independent implementations select between the identical two candidate outputs using non-semantic input features (Rust: original labels; JS: quad order). (c) Accepted standards erratum - none. No labeled erratum covers this; the supplied snapshot is not an exhaustive history search. Any public claim of a specification defect or erratum is premature until a reproducer is filed with w3c/rdf-canon and acknowledged. Note also that the contradicted property is expressed in non-normative text, so the correct framing is 'the normative algorithm does not determine a unique canonical form for this dataset', not 'a MUST is violated'.
safe_next_step: Keep production at e53464c, keep PR 6095 held, keep every gate, limit, profile and property test exactly as-is, and preserve the counterexample fixture with its hash. Execute a read-only, bounded Phase-3 evidence package with no production edit and no dependency change: (1) full W3C RDFC-1.0 suite baseline against unmodified rdf-canon 0.15.3 and against the pinned JS references; (2) the 12-case order x labeling matrix on Rust (B7); (3) IdentifierIssuer inspection plus an 11+ temporary-identifier fixture (B6); (4) a first-appearance-order-flipping relabeling to test JS label-invariance (N2); (5) a bounded randomized differential campaign over small datasets comparing all quad orders and random relabelings within a fixed work budget; (6) a prior-art search across w3c/rdf-canon issues and PRs including closed and unlabeled ones plus the CG list, then file minimal .nq reproducers upstream at zkp-ld/rdf-canon and at w3c/rdf-canon; (7) test at least two further independent implementations to see whether the tie is handled uniformly. Deliver an options paper to root; do not implement. On unblocking: the repository should stay blocked, or be unblocked only by an explicit, dated, owner-signed risk acceptance recorded in issue 6475 that names this single input, keeps the invariance property enabled for all other inputs, and carries an expiry - I do not recommend any quarantine, and any such marker is a documented policy decision by the owner, not a technical fix and not something I endorse.
repair_constraints: Must not alter canonical output for any input whose canonical form is currently unambiguous across implementations; byte-level output regression corpus required.
Must not special-case this dataset, hash, shape, or size, and must not depend on input quad order, original blank node labels, map iteration order, timing, or retries.
Must not reject ties that arise from genuine automorphism (test021c and similar must remain byte-identical passes).
Any rule that selects one of the two tie candidates is a canonical-output change and requires upstream/WG alignment first; it is out of scope for a local patch.

A fail-closed option must be conditioned on demonstrated divergence of the resulting serialization, must return a typed, documented error rather than a silent alternate output, and must be bounded with an explicit budget that itself fails closed on exhaustion - never an unbounded permutation or isomorphism search.

Any self-check design (for example canonicalizing a deterministically relabeled and reordered copy and comparing) is a detector, not a correction: it can miss ambiguities where both runs coincide, doubles cost, and must be deterministic. I am not endorsing it; it is listed only as an option to be evaluated in the options paper.
Prefer the fix upstream; if a fork or seam-level guard is unavoidable it must be clearly marked, divergence documented in interop notes, and reverted when upstream lands.

API/semver consequence must be stated explicitly: inputs that previously succeeded may now error, which changes the fallibility contract for every caller and every downstream consumer of the canonical bytes; owners must assess those consumers before adoption.
No relaxation of existing tests, gates, poison budgets or profiles as part of any repair.
validation_requirements: Complete W3C RDFC-1.0 test suite, before and after, on Rust and on the pinned references, with per-fixture results published.
Byte-level canonical-output regression corpus captured from the unmodified baseline; zero diffs required outside the explicitly enumerated newly-erroring set.
Full order x labeling invariance matrix for the counterexample and for a randomized corpus, asserting equality of canonical output under quad permutation and blank node renaming.
The existing Sparq invariance property test retained unweakened, plus a new pinned regression fixture for this pair.
Explicit enumeration and review of every input class that changes from success to error, with default-budget behaviour documented for both implementations.
Poison-dataset and work-budget tests unchanged and re-run; overhead measured against the current budget so §7.1 mitigations are not silently loosened or tightened.
Cross-implementation agreement check against at least two independent implementations on the regression corpus.
Upstream and W3C ticket references recorded in the issue and changelog before merge is considered.
Independent re-review of the actual patch, harness and results; this review covers evidence only.
public_statement: We are investigating a reproducible case in which two N-Quads serializations of the same RDF dataset - differing only in blank node labels or in quad order - produce different RDFC-1.0 canonical forms in the implementations we tested when work-factor limits are raised above their defaults. Both implementations select between the same two candidate outputs. No production code, tests, gates or limits have been changed, and the related change remains held. We are completing conformance-suite and differential testing and preparing minimal reproducers for the upstream implementation maintainers and for the W3C rdf-canon maintainers. We are not claiming a specification error unless and until those maintainers confirm one, and we are making no claims about exploitability or severity while the analysis is open.
confidence: High that the packet is internally consistent and that, as presented, the pair is isomorphic, admits no b2/b3 automorphism, and yields byte-identical N-degree preimages leaving §4.4.3(5.3) undetermined - I re-derived each of these by hand. High that the observed Rust output pair differs and that both outputs are valid relabelings. Medium-high that this is shared-algorithm underdetermination rather than a Rust-only coding error (limited by B6, B7 and the thin suite coverage). Medium that the diagnosis is complete. Low on standards classification: an erratum-level claim is unsupported at present.
limitations: I executed nothing and had no repository, network or tool access; every fact is taken from the packet as data and verified only by hand-derivation and internal cross-checking. I cannot verify archive hashes, that the quoted Rust excerpts match tag 0.15.3, that the instrumentation was truly non-perturbing, that the JS package contents are unmodified, or that the 5.0.0 supplement summary reflects its underlying runs. I have no visibility into Sparq, PR 6095, CI logs, the failing property test, the API seam, or downstream consumers. Only three W3C fixtures and one Rust input order were exercised in the evidence; no Rust suite, no randomized campaign, no further implementations. The errata snapshot is label-filtered and explicitly non-exhaustive, so novelty of the standards observation is unestablished. Nothing here approves an edit, a merge, a dependency change or a test/gate change.
